ety.text: From Middle English rasour, from Old French rasour, from raser (“to scrape, to shave”). More at rat. By surface analysis, raze + -or. Displaced the native Old English sċierseax (literally “shaving knife”).

senses.d: A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or other parts of the body.
Any tool or instrument designed for shaving.
ex: The box was jam packed full o' gifts for each manjack of us: razors, aftershave, toothbrushes, an' books.

senses.d: The sharp tusk of a wild boar.
A conceptual device that allows one to shave away unlikely explanations for a phenomenon.

ex: He thought likewise, that what with razoring and tanning, and the change of his clothes, he was not likely to be recognised.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French rasuir, from Late Latin rasōrium, from Latin rāsus (“shaved”). By surface analysis, raser + -oir.
From Late Latin rāsōrium, from Latin rāsum, rāsus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *navācla, from Latin novācula (“razor”), from Proto-Italic *(ks)nowātlā. Compare Portuguese navalha, Galician navalla, Asturian navaya.

From Old Galician-Portuguese navalla, inherited from Vulgar Latin *navac(u)la, from Latin novācula (“a sharp knife, dagger, razor”). Doublet of novácula. Cognate with Catalan and Galician navalla, Mirandese nabalha and Spanish navaja.
From cuchillo, inherited from Latin cultellus.

pt:presa.gl: prey (that which may be seized by animals)

ety.text: Feminine of preso (“imprisoned; captured; bound; prisoner”), from Old Galician-Portuguese preso, from Latin prehēnsus (“seized”), perfect passive participle of prehendō (“to seize; to catch”).
